findings.paper_title: Annex 4 - TMBC Treasury Management Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Capital expenditure underspent by £1,784k (24%) against budget in 2025/26.
findings.detail: Planned capital expenditure of £7,455k was not achieved, with actual spending of £5,671k. This represents a significant variance of approximately 24% of the planned capital programme, suggesting capital projects may be delayed or cancelled.
findings.matters: Material capital underspend indicates the council may not be progressing its capital investment programme as planned, which affects its capacity to deliver improvements and may signal project delivery or prioritization issues.
findings.figures: Budget £7,455k; Actual £5,671k; Underspend £1,784k
findings.quote: Capital expenditure 2025/26 Original 7,455 2025/26 Actual 5,671

findings.paper_title: Annex 4 - TMBC Treasury Management Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Multi-asset and property fund investments show ongoing unrealised capital losses despite some recovery.
findings.detail: Multi-asset diversified income funds show unrealised capital loss of £351,320 at 31 March 2026, an improvement from £517,950 at 31 March 2025. Property funds (LAPF) also show capital loss positions. Structural changes in managed investment portfolios and increased financial market volatility since 2024 are creating persistent pressure.
findings.matters: Ongoing unrealised losses signal volatility in reserve investments and market valuation risk; if conditions worsen, further crystallization of losses could impact the council's financial position.
findings.figures: Unrealised loss improvement £166,630 year-on-year; unrealised loss at March 2026 £351,320
findings.quote: Since 2024, structural changes within a number of the Council's externally managed investment portfolios, together with increased volatility and uncertainty in financial markets, have led fund managers to review and revise their strategic positions.

findings.paper_title: Annex 4 - TMBC Treasury Management Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Property fund investments crystallized £673,670 in capital losses during 2025/26 from forced disinvestments.
findings.detail: Lothbury Property Trust was wound up with a £582,020 loss. Hermes Property Fund merger on 15 August 2025 triggered involuntary disinvestment with a £91,650 loss. Both exits were outside the council's control, with fund managers not prioritizing smaller investors' positions.
findings.matters: Significant realized losses on reserve investments undermine expected income generation from treasury assets; involuntary position exits show councils have limited control over outcomes when fund restructuring occurs.
findings.figures: Lothbury loss £582,020; Hermes loss £91,650; combined £673,670
findings.quote: certain decisions taken by the fund managers, specifically the wind-up of one fund and the merger of another, were outside the Council's control. In both cases, the position of smaller investors was not prioritised, resulting in outcomes that required the Council's disinvestment from these holdings.

findings.headline: Council flags risk that Local Plan development costs may exceed budget and sufficient funding may not be secured
findings.detail: Risk #7 identifies that overall increases in Local Plan development costs could occur while 'additional / sufficient budget not being available and / or agreed'. Unmitigated risk score is 20, reduced to 10 after mitigation. The risk register explicitly flags that without secured budget, consequences include inability to commission evidence, reduced plan scope, or plan abandonment.
findings.matters: Cost overruns exceeding available budget would either force abandonment of the Local Plan or require drawdown of reserves, reducing the council's financial flexibility and development control capacity
findings.figures: Risk score 20 unmitigated, 10 after mitigation; identified as requiring establishment of robust budget strategy with project and financial management oversight
findings.quote: Overall increase in costs required to progress a local plan and additional / sufficient budget not being available and / or agreed

findings.headline: Interest income £1.2m against £686k original budget, significantly outperforming due to higher interest rates and Multi-Asset fund outperformance
findings.detail: Provisional outturn shows interest income of £1,204,648 against an original budget of £686,000 – a £518,648 variance (76% higher). Even the revised budget of £991,000 was £213,648 short. The paper attributes this to two factors: interest rates remaining 'slower than anticipated' in their reduction, sustaining higher yields on deposits; and Multi-Asset Diversified Income Funds performing 'better than anticipated following uncertainty in the Marketplace.'
findings.matters: This windfall interest income is contingent on elevated interest rates that will eventually normalize; a lender must distinguish this one-off benefit from underlying financial position when assessing forward sustainability and debt capacity.
findings.figures: Interest income original budget £686,000; revised budget £991,000; outturn £1,204,648
findings.quote: Increased interest receipts due to slower than anticipated reduction in the Bank Rate, have resulted in sustained higher interest yields on deposits.

findings.paper_title: Report of Head of Finance and Section 151 Officer
findings.headline: Council is consuming reserves to meet capital expenditure and to 'buy time' for revenue savings delivery
findings.detail: The council explicitly states that core cash reserves 'are being consumed over time to meet capital expenditure and buy time to enable the authority to deliver its revenue savings targets.' This language indicates the council is relying on reserve drawdown as a buffer while savings programmes are being implemented, rather than being able to sustain operations from current revenue.
findings.matters: A lender should understand that the council has identified revenue savings targets it needs to deliver and is using reserves as temporary cover while those savings are being realized. This is a solvency risk if the savings plan fails to deliver or is delayed.
findings.figures: No specific figures provided; reserve consumption ongoing
findings.quote: Core cash includes the Council's capital and revenue reserves which are being consumed over time to meet capital expenditure and 'buy time' to enable the authority to deliver its revenue savings targets.

findings.paper_title: Report of Head of Finance and Section 151 Officer
findings.headline: £2m property fund investment shows material capital depreciation of £264,720 but council retains it indefinitely
findings.detail: The council holds £2m in a Local Authority Pension Fund property fund purchased between 2017–2018, now valued at £1,735,280 as of 31 May 2026 (a 13% loss). The fund continues to generate dividends of approximately 4.3% annually. The council states it will only sell if 'a higher yielding opportunity is identified,' and explicitly acknowledges that property fund values 'may fall significantly' during economic downturns and that duration 'cannot be determined with certainty.'
findings.matters: A lender should note that the council is carrying an underwater long-term investment in an illiquid asset class with uncertain exit timing. If economic conditions deteriorate further, capital losses could increase and selling to raise cash would crystallize losses.
findings.figures: Purchase price £2m, sale value 31 May 2026 £1,735,280, loss of £264,720
findings.quote: During a downturn in the economy, capital values may fall significantly. The duration of a property fund investment may need to be extended to avoid crystalising a loss and consequently the investment's duration cannot be determined with certainty.

findings.paper_title: Report of Head of Finance and Section 151 Officer
findings.headline: Investment returns significantly outperformed budget but remain highly dependent on future interest rate movements
findings.detail: The council earned £382,700 from cash balances to May 2026, exceeding the original forecast by £535,680 and the revised estimate by £256,180. The council attributes this to slower-than-anticipated Bank Rate reductions, but explicitly notes that future income is uncertain: market expectations show rates will continue to fall eventually, and future returns are subject to 'changes in the level of reserves and changes in Bank Rate.'
findings.matters: A lender needs to know that the council's Medium Term Financial Strategy is dependent on investment income streams that are vulnerable to interest rate movements outside its control. If rates fall as currently expected, this income will decline significantly.
findings.figures: £256,180 better than revised estimate, £535,680 better than original estimate, £382,700 earned to May 2026
findings.quote: Income in future years forms part of the Council's Medium Term Financial Strategy and is subject to changes in the level of reserves and changes in Bank Rate.

findings.paper_title: Annex 4 - TMBC Treasury Management Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Multi-asset fund portfolio carries £351,320 unrealised capital loss
findings.detail: The council holds £4.25m in multi-asset diversified income funds showing an unrealised capital loss of £351,320 at 31 March 2026. While this improved from £517,950 the prior year (a £166,630 reduction), the portfolio remains in loss and exposed to ongoing market volatility.
findings.matters: The council is holding volatile equity-linked investments despite carrying nil debt; a lender would question the rationale and assess risk exposure if market conditions deteriorate.
findings.figures: Unrealised capital loss: £351,320 (prior year £517,950). Funds invested: £4.25m. Fund value: £3.89m. Annual dividend income: £203,960 (4.80% annualised return).
findings.quote: As at 31 March 2026, the Council's capital investment continues to show an unrealised capital loss of £351,320 when compared with the original investment value. This represented a significant improvement on the position reported at 31 March 2025, when the unrealised loss stood at £517,950, a reduction in the loss of £166,630 over the year.

findings.paper_title: Annex 4 - TMBC Treasury Management Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Two property fund investments were involuntarily exited with combined capital losses of £673,670
findings.detail: Hermes Property Fund merged with L&G Pensions in August 2025, forcing the council to disinvest with a capital loss of £91,650. Lothbury Property Trust was terminated in May 2024 following investor withdrawals, resulting in a capital loss of £582,020. Both exits were outside the council's control, demonstrating vulnerability to fund manager decisions.
findings.matters: A lender assessing creditworthiness needs to understand whether the council faces uncontrolled risks in its investment portfolio and whether fund volatility or forced exits could generate future cashflow pressure.
findings.figures: Hermes loss: £91,650 on redemption of £908,350. Lothbury loss: £582,020 on recovery of £1,417,980 against £5m initial investment.
findings.quote: Hermes Property Fund merged with L&G Pensions on 15 August 2025, which prompted an involuntary disinvestment of the Council's holding in the fund. The capital realisation amounted to £908,350, giving rise to a capital loss of £91,650, which will be offset by an earmarked reserve for long and medium term investments.

findings.headline: External audit identified bank reconciliation control failures; unreconciled balances and cumulative differences not investigated promptly
findings.detail: Audit found unreconciled trivial balance in Collection Deposit Book and cumulative running differences throughout year not investigated timely. Attributed to staff illness and system upgrade. Now remediated: monthly reconciliation now in place with prompt investigation of discrepancies.
findings.matters: Shows control weaknesses in basic financial governance; though resolved, indicates control environment gaps that external audit had to surface
findings.figures: Balance described as trivial
findings.quote: During our review of cash and cash equivalents, we identified an unreconciled trivial balance in the cash account, which represents the Council's Collection Deposit Book. Furthermore, there has been a cumulative running difference throughout the year that was not investigated or reconciled in a timely manner.

findings.headline: Government decarbonisation funding withdrawn; council must find alternative sources for capital climate initiatives
findings.detail: Council notes withdrawal of government funding for decarbonisation and is working to strengthen its approach to identifying and securing alternative funding. Plans to align capital and transformation programmes with defined outcome indicators to justify continued investment.
findings.matters: Loss of expected external funding source; signals capital programme changes and increased pressure on internal budgets to sustain climate commitments
findings.figures: None specified
findings.quote: In light of the withdrawal of government funding for decarbonisation initiatives, continue to progress delivery against climate change objectives by strengthening alignment between capital and transformation programmes and clearly defined, measurable outcome indicators.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation reserve established with additions planned for next two years as major projects strain resources
findings.detail: Council has created an LGR reserve and scheduled further financial additions for 2026/27 and 2027/28. Explicitly acknowledges that Refuse contract, Leisure Centre replacement, and LGR will put financial and staffing resources under pressure, requiring close oversight and potential reallocation by Corporate Management Team.
findings.matters: Shows the council expects material costs from LGR and other major projects, and is managing reserves to cover them; signals resource constraints ahead
findings.figures: LGR reserve established; further additions scheduled 2026/27 and 2027/28
findings.quote: The Council anticipates pressure from major projects (Refuse contract, Leisure Centre replacement, Local Government Reorganisation (LGR)) meaning that both financial and staffing resources will be under pressure to deliver. The Council has established a LGR reserve with further financial additions scheduled for 2026/27 and 2027/28 in order to assist with the Authorities costs.

findings.paper_title: Annex 1 - Internal Audit and Counter Fraud progress report and annual opinion for 2025/26
findings.headline: Fraud losses identified: £91,733 actual, £219,002 prevented over 3 years
findings.detail: Counter-fraud work identified actual losses of £91,733 across 2025-26 (primarily from benefits and council tax fraud). Prevented future losses over the next three years total £219,002. The majority of referrals (55) relate to Council Tax Reduction and DWP benefits fraud; 48 to Single Person Discount. This indicates material fraud exposure.
findings.matters: Actual and prevented fraud losses indicate weaknesses in income controls and housing/benefits administration; the scale suggests ongoing vulnerability.
findings.figures: 170 fraud referrals in 2025-26; £91,733 actual losses; £219,002 prevented losses; 55 referrals for Council Tax Reduction/DWP benefits, 48 for Single Person Discount
findings.quote: For 2025-26, 118 referrals have been closed. This has identified a total of £91,733 in actual loss across the fraud types, with full recovery occurring where overpayments have been identified. There is a prevented loss of £219,002 over the next 3 years.

findings.paper_title: Annex 1 - Internal Audit and Counter Fraud progress report and annual opinion for 2025/26
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation debt management: multiple high and medium-risk actions unresolved
findings.detail: Four separate management actions on temporary accommodation debt management remain overdue or outstanding, including a High Risk action on managing TA debt while debtors still occupy the accommodation. One action was marked as 'not yet commenced' as of May 2026. The council has retargeted implementation to May 2027.
findings.matters: Unresolved TA debt management is a potential revenue collection issue; repeated overdue actions suggest systemic difficulty in the revenue/housing interface.
findings.figures: High-risk action overdue since 31/03/2026, additional Medium-risk action also unresolved, new target May 2027
findings.quote: Position statement on progress to date has been provided. Follow up audit scheduled for Q4 [for Management of TA Debt - while debtor still lives in TA, dated 04/07/2025]

findings.paper_title: Annex 1 - Internal Audit and Counter Fraud progress report and annual opinion for 2025/26
findings.headline: Management implementing only 13 of 31 closed actions fully; others risk-accepted or superseded
findings.detail: Of 31 management actions closed since July 2025, only 13 were actually fully implemented. The remainder were either risk-accepted by management (14 actions) or superseded (4 actions). This approach masks the true extent of control implementation failures.
findings.matters: Risk acceptance without implementation means control weaknesses remain unresolved; superseded actions suggest the original problem has not been properly fixed.
findings.figures: 31 closed actions: 13 fully implemented, 4 superseded, 14 risk-accepted
findings.quote: Of the 31 issues closed, 13 were fully implemented (12 Medium and 1 High) 4 were superseded (all Medium) and 14 were risk accepted (2 High and 12 Medium).

findings.paper_title: Annex 1 - Internal Audit and Counter Fraud progress report and annual opinion for 2025/26
findings.headline: 10 management actions remain overdue, including 1 High-risk item on temporary accommodation debt
findings.detail: Despite improved closure rates overall, 10 agreed management actions have not been implemented by their agreed deadline, including one High Risk action on management of temporary accommodation (TA) debt while debtors still live in TA. Notably, many of the longest-standing overdue issues date back to 2023 and have received revised target dates pushed to May 2027.
findings.matters: Overdue high-risk management actions indicate management is not effectively implementing audit remediation; the TA debt issue suggests a revenue collection problem the council cannot quickly resolve.
findings.figures: 10 overdue actions (1 High, 9 Medium); one TA debt issue overdue since July 2025, one Digital Strategy item retargeted to May 2027 from October 2025
findings.quote: There are currently 30 open management actions. 10 of these are overdue/past their agreed management implementation date.

findings.paper_title: Annex 1 - Internal Audit and Counter Fraud progress report and annual opinion for 2025/26
findings.headline: Sharp increase in audit findings: 48 recommendations raised vs 29 in prior year
findings.detail: Internal audit raised 48 recommendations across 2025-26 audits, including 2 High Risk findings (up from 1), 22 Medium Risk (up from 14), and 24 Low Risk (up from 14). The increase in both volume and risk rating indicates emerging or worsening control weaknesses.
findings.matters: Growing numbers of audit findings suggest emerging control failures; the increase in High Risk issues is particularly material to lending decisions.
findings.figures: 48 recommendations total (2 High, 22 Medium, 24 Low) vs 29 in 2024-25 (1 High, 14 Medium, 14 Low)
findings.quote: There have been 48 recommendations raised for 2025-26 Audits (2 High Risk, 22 Medium Risk and 24 Low Risk) This is greater than the 29 recommendations raised for 2024-25 in all risk classification categories.

findings.paper_title: Annex 1 - Internal Audit and Counter Fraud progress report and annual opinion for 2025/26
findings.headline: Overall assurance opinion downgraded: Adequate (vs Substantial in prior year)
findings.detail: Internal Audit assigned Adequate overall assurance in 2025-26, down from Substantial in 2024-25. The number of audits receiving Substantial assurance fell from 60% to 28.57%, and there were no audits awarded High assurance, compared to one in the prior year. This represents a material weakening in control environment assessment.
findings.matters: A downgrade in the overall audit opinion signals deteriorating governance and control quality, a key metric lenders use to assess financial risk.
findings.figures: Substantial audits: 4 (28.57%) in 2025-26 vs 6 (60%) in 2024-25; High audits: 0 (0%) vs 1 (10%)
findings.quote: The audit reviews awarded Substantial (4 audits/28.57%) is a reduction from the 6 audits/60% in 2024-25, and there have been no audit reviews awarded High this year against 1 audit/10% last year. Audits awarded Adequate (10 audits/71.43%) assurance is an increase from the 2 audits/20% with this assurance level during 2024-25.

findings.headline: Property & Multi Asset Fund reserve drawn down by £2m
findings.detail: The council withdrew £2,000,000 from the Property & Multi Asset Fund Reserve in 2025/26. No detail is provided on the purpose of this drawdown, whether it is linked to the Lothbury Property Trusts loss, or how much remains in the reserve.
findings.matters: Large reserve drawdowns reduce liquidity and financial flexibility. A lender would want to know the purpose and whether further drawdowns are planned, particularly in light of the investment fund losses and property impairments in the year.
findings.figures: £2,000,000 withdrawal from Property & Multi Asset Fund Reserve
findings.quote: Property & Multi Asset Fund Reserve (2,000,000) (2,000,000) —

findings.headline: Regeneration of Tonbridge reserve contribution increased to £8.45m, above budget
findings.detail: Contributions to the Regeneration of Tonbridge earmarked reserve exceeded budget significantly: original estimate £6.7m, revised estimate £7.7m, actual £8.45m. This represents a £750k increase against the revised budget and suggests accelerated or expanded regeneration commitments. The reserve is being built up for future spend on town centre regeneration and related initiatives.
findings.matters: Large reserve contributions for regeneration commit future cash and may indicate the council is front-loading funding for long-term projects. A lender would want to see delivery plans and timescales for these committed funds to assess cash flow risk.
findings.quote: Regeneration of Tonbridge (6,700,000) (7,700,000) (8,450,000)

findings.headline: Maintenance and repairs work deferred to 2026/27 building backlog
findings.detail: Multiple items of planned building maintenance and repair work were pushed into the next financial year: roof repair at council offices (£5k), bin compound creation at Tonbridge Castle (£6k), maisonettes repairs for temporary accommodation (£40k), and community areas maintenance (£19k). These are noted as 'slipped' or 'deferred', suggesting either budget constraint, prioritisation, or project delay.
findings.matters: Deferring routine maintenance work can accumulate into larger, more costly problems. Repeated deferrals signal either capital constraint or facility management issues. Maisonettes repairs deferral is particularly relevant to homelessness accommodation capacity.
findings.figures: Roof repair £5k, bin compound £6k, maisonettes £40k, community areas £19k deferred to 2026/27
findings.quote: Roof repair work (£5k) and creation of a bin compound at Tonbridge Castle (£6k) have been slipped to 2026/27.

findings.headline: Homelessness accommodation rental income £78k below revised budget
findings.detail: Customer & Client Receipts from temporary accommodation fell to £863,900 (provisional) against a revised budget of £1,054,500—a shortfall of £190,600. The document notes: 'The rental income budget for temporary accommodation was calculated as an average of the year to date income, actual income has proven to be a lot lower than the budgeted rental income.' A separate note adds: 'Lower than anticipated rental income due to properties requiring essential maintenance and therefore being void for a longer period than projected.'
findings.matters: Void periods and lower-than-expected rental income from temporary accommodation signal either operational issues (maintenance backlogs, void management) or a shortfall in placements. Either is a concern for councils facing homelessness demand.
findings.figures: Revised budget £1,054,500; actual £863,900; shortfall £190,600 (18%)
findings.quote: The rental income budget for temporary accommodation was calculated as an average of the year to date income, actual income has proven to be a lot lower than the budgeted rental income.

findings.headline: Bad debt provisions rising sharply across benefits and waste services
findings.detail: The council increased bad debt provisions in multiple areas: Housing Benefits contribution to bad debt provision rose from £153,050 budgeted to £272,490 actual—an increase of 78%. Garden waste bad debt provision jumped from £5,000 budgeted to £93,000 actual (an increase of 1,760%). The Housing Benefits note cites 'reassessment of the bad debts provision on overpayments, having regard to the age and size of the debt and level of write-offs.' For garden waste, 'the level of garden waste debt has increased considerably; the impairment allowance has been increased to reflect the likelihood of debt collection having regard to the age and size of the debt.'
findings.matters: Rising bad debt provisions indicate either deteriorating collection performance, growing debtor age, or a reappraisal of collection likelihood. This signals weakening cash recovery and may reflect household affordability pressure (benefits) or service uptake issues (garden waste).
findings.quote: The level of garden waste debt has increased considerably, the impairment allowance has been increased to reflect the likelihood of debt collection having regard to the age and size of the debt.

findings.headline: Parking services income £2.27m above revised budget — unusual scale and source unclear
findings.detail: Parking services generated £3,857,167 in income (provisional outturn) versus a revised budget of £1,584,350, a positive variance of £2,273,000 or 143%. The summary shows the line as a credit of (3,857,167), the largest single swing in the directorate. No detail in the document explains the driver of this exceptional outperformance. The document does not separate the causes—whether from increased enforcement, higher penalty charges, new parking schemes, or other sources.
findings.matters: An unexplained income surge of this scale raises questions about sustainability, accuracy, and underlying operations. A lender would want to verify whether this is recurring (e.g. a new paid parking scheme now running) or one-off, and whether the cash has been realised.
findings.figures: £1,584,350 budgeted; £3,857,167 actual; variance +£2,273,000

findings.headline: Lothbury Property Trusts investment fund terminated, crystallising £673k loss
findings.detail: The council held an investment in Lothbury Property Trusts, a pooled property fund. The decision was made to 'terminate the fund after consultation with stakeholders', resulting in an actual loss of £673,679 (budgeted loss was £750,000). This loss sits in Investment Fund Losses within Treasury Management and Banking.
findings.matters: Fund terminations typically indicate underlying asset quality or governance issues. A lender would want to know the rationale, whether this reflects a wider reassessment of property investment strategy, and how much of the original capital was lost.
findings.figures: £673,679 loss on Lothbury Property Trusts termination; budgeted £750,000
findings.quote: Lower than originally anticipated capital investment loss resulting from the Lothbury Property Trusts decision, after consultation with stakeholders, to terminate the fund.

findings.headline: Gibson East building revalued downward with £1.67m impairment loss
findings.detail: The Gibson East building incurred a non-current asset impairment of £1,665,608 following revaluation in the year. The building was vacant during refurbishment and the authority received temporary rates relief. No detail given on whether impairment reflects structural issues, cost overruns on works, or market conditions. The only note is: 'Reflects impairment of Gibson East building following revaluation.'
findings.matters: Material write-downs on council property signal potential issues with asset quality, capital delivery, or market values. A lender would want to understand the causes and whether other properties carry similar impairment risk.
findings.figures: £1,665,608 impairment charge; building vacant during year for refurbishment
findings.quote: Reflects impairment of Gibson East building following revaluation.

findings.headline: Regen of Tonbridge Reserve increased 2.7x with £8.45m contribution
findings.detail: The reserve for regeneration projects grew from £4.32m to £11.58m following an £8.45m contribution in 2025/26. This substantial increase signals major capital commitments or projects entering delivery phase.
findings.matters: Large buildups in capital reserves indicate future spending commitments and signal the council's debt and funding strategy, which affects borrowing capacity and financial forecasts.

findings.headline: Tonbridge & Malling Leisure Trust Reserve completely exhausted in one year
findings.detail: The entire £286,200 reserve earmarked for the Leisure Trust was withdrawn in 2025/26, leaving a zero balance. Complete depletion of a designated reserve in a single year is unusual and warrants explanation.
findings.matters: Total drawdown of a named reserve suggests either a one-time capital event, sustained subsidy requirement, or fundamental change in the underlying entity's financial position.
findings.figures: Opening £286,200.00; withdrawn £286,200.00; closing £0.00
findings.quote: Tonbridge & Malling Leisure Trust 286,200.00 (286,200.00) 0.00

findings.headline: Domestic Abuse reserve overspent and now shows negative balance
findings.detail: The Domestic Abuse reserve was drawn by £82,410 despite having only £78,302 available, resulting in a negative closing balance of £4,108. This indicates spending exceeded both the budget and the reserve provision.
findings.matters: A reserve going negative signals either inadequate budget planning or loss of control over a specific service expenditure, both of which are red flags for financial governance.

findings.headline: Budget Stabilisation Reserve drawn down by 94% in a single year
findings.detail: The Budget Stabilisation Reserve fell from £2.87m to £412k, with £2.71m drawn in 2025/26. This reserve exists to absorb budget volatility, and its near-exhaustion indicates the council faced significant budget pressures during the year.
findings.matters: A depleted stabilisation reserve limits the council's ability to absorb future budget shocks, which is a core measure of financial resilience that lenders assess.

findings.paper_title: Annex 6 - Medium Term Financial Strategy - May 2026
findings.headline: Council tax funding is planned to grow 44% over the decade, relying on consistent 3% annual increases every single year.
findings.detail: Council tax revenue grows from £13,813k in 2026/27 to £19,899k in 2035/36. The MTFS assumes a 3.0% increase without variation every year for ten consecutive years, which becomes a material assumption by the end of the period.
findings.matters: Heavy reliance on council tax increases is politically difficult to sustain, especially at a uniform 3% annually. Capped increases or resident resistance would force further service cuts or reserves depletion.

findings.paper_title: Annex 6 - Medium Term Financial Strategy - May 2026
findings.headline: Total usable reserves decline by 46% over ten years, from £12.2m to £6.5m.
findings.detail: Reserves start at £12,158k in 2026/27 and decline to £6,505k by 2035/36, dropping to a low of £5,565k in 2033/34 before modest recovery. This represents significant erosion of the council's financial buffer.
findings.matters: A lender would be concerned about declining reserves as they reduce headroom to manage demand shocks, unexpected costs, or revenue shortfalls, and may indicate structural overspending.

findings.paper_title: Annex 6 - Medium Term Financial Strategy - May 2026
findings.headline: A planned draw of £5.1m from reserves in 2027/28 signals acute budget pressure that single year.
findings.detail: Revenue reserves contribute £5,079k to funding in 2027/28, a sharp reversal from the £665k addition planned for 2026/27 and a material draw. This is driven by the collapse in investment income. Reserves continue to be drawn in subsequent years at a smaller scale.
findings.matters: A large reserve draw suggests the council cannot fund planned spending through normal revenues and must use reserves as a temporary buffer. It signals financial pressure and reduces resilience for future shocks.
findings.figures: Revenue Reserves funding swing: -665 (2026/27), then 5,079 (2027/28), then declining draws through the decade

findings.paper_title: Annex 6 - Medium Term Financial Strategy - May 2026
findings.headline: Investment income collapses by 59% in the first three years, from £2.1m to £846k annually.
findings.detail: Investment income falls from £2,071k in 2026/27 to £846k in 2028/29, then stabilizes around £700–715k. This loss of approximately £1.2m in annual recurring income is the primary driver of budget pressure in 2027/28 and materially worsens the council's financial position going forward.
findings.matters: Investment income is a discretionary revenue source. A sudden 59% drop signals either a material change in the council's cash position or investment strategy and significantly erodes financial flexibility to manage future pressures.

findings.paper_title: Annex 6 - Medium Term Financial Strategy - May 2026
findings.headline: Borrowing for new capital schemes is stated as required but the amounts and funding source are not shown.
findings.detail: The MTFS title declares that borrowing for new schemes is required. However, the capital provision line shows only £500k annually in 2026/27-2027/28, then £250k in 2028/29, then zero. Capital charges (likely including debt servicing) rise from £2,952k to £3,564k over the decade, but no explicit borrowing figures appear in the funding section, suggesting the borrowing is planned but not yet quantified.
findings.matters: A lender would need to understand the scale and repayment profile of planned borrowing, whether debt capacity exists, and how capital schemes will be prioritised and funded.
findings.figures: Capital Charges: £2,952k (2026/27) to £3,564k (2035/36); Provision for new Capital Schemes: £500k, £500k, £250k, then £0
findings.quote: Borrowing for new schemes required.

findings.headline: Homelessness service and temporary accommodation spending increasing, with large capital commitments planned.
findings.detail: The council is undertaking a 'Temporary Accommodation & Resettlement Scheme' with capital spending of £1.2m in 2026/27 and £3.471m in 2027/28, funded from 'Local Authority Housing Fund, S106 and TA Earmarked Reserves', with completion due March 2027. The MTFS shows assumed increases in temporary accommodation provision of £100k in 2027/28 rising to £200k in 2028/29. Homelessness revenue budget was £1,291k in 2025/26 and is £1,386k in 2026/27. This suggests a structurally growing demand area being funded from time-limited government schemes and council reserves.
findings.matters: Homelessness is a growing national social pressure. Councils funding this from one-off grants and reserves rather than baseline funding face a structural affordability risk when external funding ends. Large capital outlays with uncertain future revenue funding indicate a service under pressure.
findings.quote: The delivery of the resettlement properties and temporary accommodation through use of the Local Authority Housing Fund, S106 and TA Earmarked Reserves continues to be delivered with the project completion now due for March 2027. Delivery will be achieved through the repurposing of existing Council accommodation, open market, or housing provider property purchases, as well as the Blue Bell Hill modular housing scheme.

findings.headline: General Revenue Reserve declining from £12.3m (2026/27) to £4.6m (2035/36), approaching the £2m minimum floor.
findings.detail: The council's Medium Term Financial Strategy projects the General Revenue Reserve will decline steadily from £12,338k at the end of 2026/27 to £4,619k by 2035/36. The council's stated objective is to 'retain a minimum of £3.0m in the General Revenue Reserve by the end of the strategy period and not to fall below £2.0m at any time during the 10-year period'. The projection shows headroom of only £2.6m above the absolute minimum by year 10, with the reserve declining in most years.
findings.matters: Reserves are the council's buffer against unexpected costs, service failures, or income shortfalls. A reserve that declines to near-minimum over the planning period leaves the council with little capacity to absorb adverse variations and may force service cuts if assumptions slip.
findings.figures: Reserves 2026/27: £12,338k; Reserves 2035/36: £4,619k; Minimum threshold: £2,000k; Target at end of strategy: £3,000k
findings.quote: To retain a minimum of £3.0m in the General Revenue Reserve by the end of the strategy period and not to fall below £2.0m at any time during the 10-year period.

findings.headline: External auditor identified a procurement weakness in internal control arrangements; improvement plans being monitored.
findings.detail: Following the 2024/25 audit, Grant Thornton concluded the authority has 'proper arrangements to secure economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources'. However, one weakness 'in arrangements covering Procurement remains and improvement plans are now in place and are being monitored'. This is the only control weakness flagged in the audit conclusion, indicating a specific governance gap in how the council manages supplier spend and procurement discipline.
findings.matters: Procurement weakness is a common source of cost overrun, fraud, or wasteful spend in local authorities. For a lender, an auditor-flagged weakness in this area suggests elevated risk of overspending or poor value on major projects (including the Angel Centre).
findings.figures: One weakness identified; no financial impact quantified
findings.quote: Following the 2024/25 audit, our external auditor (Grant Thornton UK LLP) concluded the Authority has put in place proper arrangements to secure economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources. One weakness in arrangements covering Procurement remains and improvement plans are now in place and are being monitored.

findings.headline: Kent Business Rates Pool dissolving from end of 2025/26, removing pooling gains as a future income source.
findings.detail: The council participated in the Kent Business Rates Pool, which generated gains through the pooling mechanism. The pool is dissolving at the end of 2025/26 due to 'changes in baseline levels and risks surrounding growth in rateable values'. The document states this 'does not preclude the reformation in later years subject to Government approval', signalling that pooling gains can no longer be relied upon and future reformation is uncertain.
findings.matters: Loss of an intermittent but valuable income source (the 2025/26 budget shows pool gains of £428,688) removes flexibility. Combined with the baseline reset that absorbed all prior growth, this leaves the council with no upside from local business rate performance.
findings.quote: Due to the changes in baseline levels and risks surrounding growth in rateable values from 2026/27 the Kent Business Rates Pool to the decision to dissolve the pool from the end of the 2025/26 Financial Year. This does not preclude the reformation in later years subject to Government approval.

findings.headline: Government grant funding falls £866,000 by 2028/29 due to Fair Funding Review and Business Rates Reset absorbing all prior growth.
findings.detail: The council's grant settlement declined £100,247 in 2026/27 (1.1% cut). Over the three-year settlement period to 2028/29, the council receives £866,000 less than the 2025/26 baseline. This reflects deliberate policy: the Fair Funding Review rolled together multiple grants and reset business rates baselines, explicitly absorbing all previous business rate growth that the council had accumulated. The document notes this was the 'second largest reduction in Core Spending Power' among all councils.
findings.matters: Structural government funding declines are a key indicator of financial stress for local authorities. This council faces an unusually large cut that persists into future years, reducing financial flexibility at a time when social pressures (homelessness) are growing.
findings.figures: £9,062,754 grant settlement 2026/27 (down from £9,163,001 in 2025/26); £866,000 reduction by 2028/29; Business rates down from £5,324,504 to £3,362,707 (36.8% fall)
findings.quote: the Council will receive £866,000 less in 2028/29 when compared to the notional amount for 2025/26. These amounts could also be subject to alteration in 2027/28 to take account of changes in the Councils Rateable Value of Business Rate premises on 31st March 2026.

findings.headline: Angel Centre leisure replacement project costs £19.4 million with final approval deferred to Autumn 2026.
findings.detail: The council is planning a major replacement leisure centre at an estimated cost of £19.4m based on RIBA Stage 2 completion. Funding is to come from a combination of council reserves, external borrowing, and contributions from the Leisure Trust and developers. The final decision on whether the project will proceed has been deferred to Autumn 2026, creating material uncertainty over a capital commitment representing 77% of the council's estimated total capital spending over the next two years (2026/27-2027/28: £1.4m + £15m).
findings.matters: A lender assessing the council's financial stability needs to understand whether this project will proceed and on what borrowing terms. If it proceeds, it materially affects the council's debt position and affordability; if deferred, it signals reconsideration of a long-standing commitment.
findings.figures: £19.4 million estimated cost (RIBA Stage 2), £1.4m budgeted 2026/27, £15m budgeted 2027/28, £3m budgeted 2028/29
findings.quote: A major project is underway to replace the existing Angel Leisure Centre with a new, state-of-the-art Leisure Centre located on the Sovereign Way Mid Car Park. The estimated cost of the project is currently around £19.4 million, based on the completion of RIBA Stage 2. Funding for the development is expected to come from a combination of sources, including funds held by the Council, external borrowing, and external contributions from the Leisure Trust and developer funding. A final decision on whether the project will proceed will be made by Full Council in Autumn 2026.

findings.paper_title: Annex 16a Robustness of Estimates and Adequacy of Reserves Statement 2627
findings.headline: Angel Centre replacement is a material capital commitment still in development without finalised business case or funding
findings.detail: The Angel Centre replacement has been agreed in principle but officers have not finalised the business case or funding arrangements. The Capital Strategy includes intentions to earmark funds to support development costs, but final project approval remains pending.
findings.matters: Major capital schemes without final business case or funding plan represent contingent exposure; scope or cost changes mid-delivery can force reserve drawdown or borrowing decisions
findings.figures: Annual capital allowance £500k until 2027/28; specific project funding unquantified pending finalisation
findings.quote: Whilst the replacement to the Angel Centre in Tonbridge has been agreed in principle, officers are yet to finalise the business case and funding arrangements for the final project approval by Members.

findings.paper_title: Annex 16a Robustness of Estimates and Adequacy of Reserves Statement 2627
findings.headline: The balanced position depends entirely on three specific savings of £800k that council flags as fragile assumptions
findings.detail: The nil funding gap relies on: office accommodation scaling-back (£200k), increased council-owned temporary accommodation use (£200k), and leisure trust net service fee (£400k). The S25 explicitly states 'a number of factors assumed in future years could be different and therefore the funding gap may reappear', directly flagging these assumptions carry material risk.
findings.matters: A balanced budget with no contingency is weaker than one with headroom; if any major saving fails, the council moves to deficit with limited options
findings.figures: £200k office scaling; £200k homelessness service reduction; £400k leisure income; £895k central government funding reduction by 2028/29
findings.quote: This nil position assumes that some long term reductions in cost or increased income will occur in the MTFS, namely the scaling back on office accommodation in the sum of £200,000, the increased usage of Council owned or leased temporary accommodation for Homelessness clients of £200,000 and a net income from the service fee from the Leisure Trust of £400,000... a number of factors assumed in future years could be different and therefore the funding gap may reappear.

findings.paper_title: Annex 16a Robustness of Estimates and Adequacy of Reserves Statement 2627
findings.headline: Refuse, recycling and street cleansing contract recommissioning could force rebudget and gap reassessment if costs exceed assumptions
findings.detail: The budget is built on assumed costs for refuse and street cleansing services. However, the contract recommissioning process has not concluded — results are expected after the budget is set. An adverse settlement could flip the council from balanced to deficit within weeks, requiring a further Cabinet report.
findings.matters: Refuse collection is a major fixed cost; an adverse contract can rapidly consume headroom and force reserves or borrowing decisions mid-year
findings.figures: Results expected after 2026/27 budget-setting; timing creates the risk window
findings.quote: There are further risks arising from the recommissioning of the refuse, recycling and street cleansing contract, the results of which are expected after this budget will be set, meaning that the funding gap may require reassessment early in the new financial year, with a further report being presented to Cabinet.

findings.paper_title: Annex 16a Robustness of Estimates and Adequacy of Reserves Statement 2627
findings.headline: Homelessness accommodation costs have risen significantly and managing them may require reserve drawdown
findings.detail: The council has experienced recent significant cost increases for temporary accommodation for homelessness clients. The MTFS plans to control these through providing council-owned and managed accommodation, but explicitly flags that this 'could require some reserve funding depending on the time taken to achieve these goals'. This creates operational stress in a statutory service and contingent reserve exposure.
findings.matters: Unexpected reserve drawdowns to fund statutory homelessness provision signal underlying service stress and reduce financial flexibility for other demands or shocks
findings.figures: Recent significant increases in costs; council-owned accommodation solution timeline uncertain
findings.quote: In terms of homelessness, the MTFS assumes that the recent significant increases in costs will be brought under control over the medium term through the provision of council owned and managed accommodation, the achievement of which could require some reserve funding depending on the time taken to achieve these goals.

findings.headline: Medium-term capital funding gap: borrowing may be needed beyond 2027/28
findings.detail: The annual capital allowance has been uplifted to £500,000 through 2027/28 to account for Local Government Reorganisation, up from £250,000. The council's financial projections acknowledge that once this uplift ends, borrowing may be necessary to fund capital schemes. This indicates structural capital funding pressure even before Angel Centre repayments would begin.
findings.matters: Signals that capital investment is resource-constrained and borrowing is part of the council's medium-term financial planning, not a one-off decision.
findings.figures: Capital allowance uplift: £250,000 to £500,000 through end of 2027/28; uplift ends 2027/28
findings.quote: Based on the agreed capital plan and future projections the Council may need to borrow to fund such expenditure beyond 2027/28.

findings.headline: Angel Centre replacement project (£19.4m) will require borrowing
findings.detail: The council approved a £19.4 million capital scheme for Angel Centre replacement at Full Council on 8 April 2025. The Capital Strategy confirms that borrowing will be necessary to finance part of this project. This represents the council's first material borrowing, as it currently holds no debt (nil outstanding at 31 March 2025). The council is seeking alternative financing to reduce the borrowing requirement, but the shortfall is expected.
findings.matters: A £19.4m debt commitment is material and changes the council's capital structure from no leverage. Lenders need to understand the project business case, repayment profile, and whether the revenue base can support debt service alongside existing spending.
findings.figures: £19.4 million capital cost; Debt Outstanding at 31 March 2025: Nil
findings.quote: it is likely that borrowing will be necessary in order to provide some of the financing for the project

findings.headline: Service area cost pressures across homelessness, leisure trust utilities, and waste continuing to require careful management
findings.detail: The council flags ongoing cost pressures in multiple service areas including leisure trust, utility costs, waste, and homelessness. These are described as being managed carefully but remain areas requiring active oversight. Homelessness is flagged separately with sustained demand and increased temporary accommodation costs, partially offset by £1.6m Local Authority Housing Fund and new owned/leased accommodation portfolio development.
findings.matters: These ongoing operational pressures eat into the £600k savings target. If any of these services deteriorate faster than anticipated, the first-tranche deadline becomes harder to meet.
findings.figures: £1.6m Local Authority Housing Fund received for temporary accommodation portfolio
findings.quote: Leisure Trust Utility costs Waste, Homelessness and Local Plan continue to be service areas of financial pressure and are being managed carefully.

findings.headline: Angel Leisure Centre replacement will require borrowing, reports due early 2025/26
findings.detail: The council has decided it needs to plan for potential borrowing for the replacement of Angel Leisure Centre. This is a capital commitment of unspecified value, with reports on the borrowing requirement expected in the first part of 2025/26. This represents a material fixed obligation beyond the operational savings challenge.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess total debt capacity and the timing of this borrowing against the operational deficit challenge. Angel Centre is a revenue-generating asset (trust-operated) so replacement affects both capital position and leisure trust sustainability.
findings.figures: Angel Leisure Centre replacement borrowing requirement; reports due first part 2025/26
findings.quote: Council will need to plan for potential for borrowing in relation to replacement of Angel Leisure Centre. Reports due to come to Members in first part of 2025/26.

findings.headline: £2.8m medium-term funding gap with £600k first tranche due 1 April 2026
findings.detail: The council anticipates a £2.8m funding gap over the next 4-5 years following national Funding Reform. The immediate challenge is delivering £600k of savings by April 2026, but only £300k has been identified so far. A new savings programme is being devised by Management Team with details to be reported to Cabinet.
findings.matters: A lender needs to see whether this council can execute identified savings on schedule. Only 50% of the first tranche is identified with less than 6 months to deliver.
findings.figures: £2.8m funding gap over 4-5 years; £600k first tranche by 1 April 2026; £300k identified and reported September 2025
findings.quote: expected funding gap to be £2.8m. This can be broken down into tranches over next 4 to 5 years with first tranche of £600k to be achieved by 1 April 2026. £300k has now been identified and reported to both Cabinet and FRPSSC in September 2025

findings.headline: Fixed Asset Register update from prior year remains in progress; only land and buildings reviewed to date
findings.detail: A recommendation from the 2023-24 audit to update the Fixed Asset Register is still open and in progress. Land and buildings FAR was reviewed in 2022-23 but other asset class registers remain to be reviewed. This multi-year control improvement has not progressed beyond the initial phase, suggesting resource or priority constraints.
findings.matters: Asset register completeness is fundamental to accurate financial reporting and capital asset management. Slow progress on prior-year control improvements suggests implementation challenges that could affect the council's ability to remediate other control findings.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: Work remains in progress. Recommendation remains open.

findings.headline: Bank reconciliation control weakness: unreconciled trivial balance not investigated timely throughout the year
findings.detail: The audit identified an unreconciled trivial balance in the cash account (Collection Deposit Book) and a cumulative running difference that was not investigated or resolved promptly during the year. The council attributes this to staff illness and a system upgrade. Although immaterial, this indicates a control weakness in a fundamental control. Management agrees to prioritise resolving all reconciling items timely.
findings.matters: Bank reconciliation is a key control for financial governance. Control weaknesses, even on immaterial amounts, suggest potential gaps in the control environment and cash management resilience that affect risk assessment.
findings.figures: Balance is trivial (below £74,500 reporting threshold)
findings.quote: During our review of cash and cash equivalents, we identified an unreconciled trivial balance in the cash account, which represents the Council's Collection Deposit Book. Furthermore, there has been a cumulative running difference throughout the year that was not investigated or reconciled in a timely manner.

findings.headline: Pension liability fell by £3.245m, from £6.127m to £2.882m, reducing long-term financial risk
findings.detail: The council's defined benefit pension liability improved substantially. The pension fund is now in surplus, with fund assets of £106.4m against defined benefit obligations of £97.7m. The auditor found no issues with the valuation and confirmed the judgments were appropriate. This is a material improvement in the council's financial sustainability.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities are a primary long-term financial commitment for councils. A £3.245m reduction improves the council's balance sheet and borrowing capacity, reducing financial risk for lenders and improving the council's flexibility.
findings.figures: Pension liability fell from £6.127m at 31 March 2024 to £2.882m at 31 March 2025. Fund assets £106.4m vs defined benefit obligations £97.7m.
findings.quote: The pension fund net liability is £2.882m in the Council's Balance Sheet at 31 March 2025, falling by £3.245m from £6.127m at 31 March 2024

findings.paper_title: 01 Report of Head of Finance and s151 Officer
findings.headline: £57,300 in unbudgeted emergency maintenance costs for water leak and castle grounds works
findings.detail: Emergency maintenance has been identified at the Racecourse Ground (water leak) and essential grounds maintenance works at the Castle, totalling £57,300. These costs are additional to the approved budget and will consume reserves or require virement from elsewhere.
findings.matters: Unbudgeted emergency expenditure indicates deferred or deteriorating maintenance; reduces budget flexibility for other priorities and signals possible asset management challenges.
findings.quote: The Director of Street Scene, Leisure and Technical Services has identified two additional overspends arising from a water leak at the Racecourse Ground and essential grounds maintenance works surrounding the rebutment at the Castle amounting to £57,300.

findings.paper_title: 01 Report of Head of Finance and s151 Officer
findings.headline: Business rates income forecast £60,282 below estimate due to empty properties and delayed property valuations
findings.detail: Predicted net business rates income is £4,149,489 against the original estimate of £4,209,769. The shortfall is driven by increased levels of empty business properties and awaited valuations of business properties adjacent to Junction 5 of the M20. The valuations are described as 'awaited', indicating uncertainty.
findings.matters: Material headwind in business rates—a key revenue stream—reflecting economic weakness in the commercial property market. Valuations pending for properties that may represent significant income once confirmed.
findings.figures: £4,209,769 original estimate; £4,149,489 predicted net income; £60,282 variance
findings.quote: As at the end of July the predicted net income is £4,149,489 a variation of £60,282, this is because of increased levels of empty business properties and the awaited valuations of business properties adjacent to Junction 5 of the M20.

findings.paper_title: 01 Report of Head of Finance and s151 Officer
findings.headline: £2.8m medium-term funding gap has only £302,500 identified from first £600,000 saving tranche, with further savings not yet quantified
findings.detail: The MTFS identifies a £2.8m funding gap requiring £600,000 savings across four tranches by February 2026 budget setting. From base budget reviews, the council has identified £182,500; adding a £120,000 inflation underbid on waste contracts brings the total to £302,500, just meeting a £300k milestone. However, the council is now in discussions with service directors on additional savings which are described as 'currently being collated' and to be discussed in November budget processes.
findings.matters: Only 50% of first-tranche savings identified through straightforward base budget reviews; gap-closing plan depends on an inflation windfall; additional savings remain unquantified and behind schedule entering the critical budget-setting period.
findings.figures: £2.8m total funding gap; £600,000 first-tranche target; £182,500 identified from base reviews; £120,000 inflation underbid; £302,500 total; £300,000 milestone
findings.quote: The MTFS agreed in February 2025 had a funding gap of £2.8m, this target was broken down into 4 tranches £600k to be achieved by the time the budget is set in February 2026 for the 2026/27 Budget.

findings.paper_title: 01 Report of Head of Finance and s151 Officer
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation overspend forecast to reach £180,000 by year-end if client numbers do not improve
findings.detail: Client numbers stand at 122 at end of July (down from 129 in May) against a budgeted target of 120 by year-end. Current overspend against the profiled budget is £60,000; if client numbers and placements do not change, this will grow to an estimated £180,000 full-year overspend. The report notes this was also highlighted in the prior year.
findings.matters: Material overspend in a specific service indicates either a forecasting error or genuine service delivery challenge. The council says efforts continue to reduce numbers, but progress so far is insufficient.
findings.figures: 122 clients at end July, 129 in May, 120 budgeted; £60,000 current overspend, £180,000 forecast full-year
findings.quote: As at the end of July, there is an overspend against profiled budget of circa £60,000 and therefore if the current client numbers and placements were not to change the predicted overspend against the original budget by year end would be £180,000.

news_drafts.headline: Capital expenditure underspent by £1,784k (24%) against budget in 2025/26.
news_drafts.lead: Material capital underspend indicates the council may not be progressing its capital investment programme as planned, which affects its capacity to deliver improvements and may signal project delivery or prioritization issues.

news_drafts.lead: Ongoing unrealised losses signal volatility in reserve investments and market valuation risk; if conditions worsen, further crystallization of losses could impact the council's financial position.

news_drafts.lead: Significant realized losses on reserve investments undermine expected income generation from treasury assets; involuntary position exits show councils have limited control over outcomes when fund restructuring occurs.
